newsitem.title: USA: Rudi to pay $86,331 to settle SEC fraud charges.
newsitem.headline: Rudi to pay $86,331 to settle SEC fraud charges.

text.p: Former New Jersey financial adviser Nicholas Rudi agreed to pay $86,331 to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges that he got over $200,000 in kickbacks to help steer bond underwriting business to an investment bank, SEC announced on Monday.

Rudi and his financial advisory firm, Public Capital Advisors, Inc., formerly known as Consolidated Financial Management, Inc., neither admitted or denied SEC's charges that Rudi got kickbacks from First Fidelity Securities Group in connection with a $237.5 million Camden County utilities authority offering in February 1990, SEC said.
Today's action follows an earlier setback for federal enforcement officials in the Rudi matter and in a three-year federal crackdown on alleged abuses in the $1.3 trillion municipal bond market.
A federal jury on June 4 acquitted Rudi, an adviser to former New Jersey Gov. Jim Florio, of charges that he accepted kickbacks to help First Fidelity win the 1990 New Jersey deal.

But today, the SEC announced that Rudi agreed to pay back, or "disgorge," $49,132 in profits from the 1990 deal and $37,200 in interest, in a settlement pact filed with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.
The SEC charged on February 23, 1995 that Rudi and three other individuals were involved in the kickback scheme.

The three others, who agreed simultaneously to settle the charges, were George Tuttle and Alexander Williams, former high-ranking municipal bond executives at First Fidelity Securities, and Joseph Salema, a partner of Rudi.
Tuttle and Williams agreed to disgorge $18,171 million and $4,684 in profits, respectively. Salema agreed to disgorge $324,765. Rudi refused to settle charges at the time.
First Fidelity Securities, the municipal securities dealer of First Fidelity Bank, N.A., agreed on January 9, 1996 to pay a civil fine of $2.29 million in connection with the Tuttle-Williams matter.
The securities group said the activities of Tuttle and Williams were "unauthorized and clandestine." On January 1, 1996, First Fidelity Bancorporation merged with First Union Corporation.
